chunks: From him, from al-Abbas, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Rib'i, from al-Fudayl, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

A 'khumrah' was brought to my father (peace be upon him) on the day of al-Fitr, so he ordered it to be returned. He said: 'This is a day when the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) loved to look at the horizons of the sky and to place his forehead on the ground.'

key_terms.آفَاقِ السَّمَاءِ: The horizons of the sky, referring to looking up at the heavens.
key_terms.جَبْهَتَهُ: His forehead, specifically referring to the part of the body that touches the ground in prostration (sujood).
key_terms.خُمْرَة: A type of garment or covering, often referring to a cloak or upper garment.
key_terms.رَسُولُ اللَّهِ: The Messenger of Allah (Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him and his family).
key_terms.يَوْمَ الْفِطْرِ: The day of Eid al-Fitr, the festival marking the end of Ramadan.

ai.seo_question: What did the Prophet love to do on the day of Eid al-Fitr according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) instructs the return of a 'khumrah' (likely a fine garment or head covering) on Eid al-Fitr, linking the day to the Prophet’s (peace be upon him and his family) custom of gazing at the heavens and prostrating. This practice underscores the Eid as a day of spiritual elevation and gratitude, where physical adornment is secondary to the humility of *sujood* and contemplation of the Creator. It reflects the Shia emphasis on emulating the Prophet’s specific devotional habits during festive occasions.
